title: Found an Animal on the Street

blocks.body: Not every cat you find needs to be taken home right away. But if the animal is in danger, injured, emaciated, or clearly in need of help, act calmly and methodically.

blocks.heading: Your safety first
blocks.body: Catch it only in gloves or through a towel. After a bite or a scratch, wash the wound with soap and water and see a doctor the same day.

blocks.heading: 1. First, assess the situation
blocks.body:
Before approaching the animal, make sure it is safe for both you and the cat.
Pay attention to:
• Whether there is a busy road nearby.
• Whether the cat could run out in front of a car.
• Whether there are dogs or other sources of danger nearby.
• Whether the cat is trapped (under a car, in a well, up a tree, etc.).
If the location is dangerous, first try to get the animal out of the risk zone.

blocks.heading: 2. Don't try to pick the cat up right away
3. If you manage to catch the cat
4. Check the animal's condition (keep in mind it may be in shock from being caught)
5. Don't feed it heavily right away
blocks.body:
A very hungry cat should not be abruptly fed a large amount of food.
If the animal is weak:
• offer a small amount of water first;
• then a small portion of wet food.
Do not give: milk; sausage; bones; food from the table.

blocks.heading: 6. If the cat is injured
7. Don't introduce it to your own pets right away
8. Visit a veterinary clinic
9. Try to find the owner
10. If you decide to keep the cat
When you need to go to the veterinarian immediately
Important tip
blocks.body:
Even if the cat you found seems tame and healthy, don't let it back out onto the street right after catching it.
First check for a microchip and try to find the owner through veterinary clinics, shelters, and local communities. If no owner is found, the animal will still need a veterinary checkup, quarantine, and parasite treatment before being introduced to other pets.

title: Found a Kitten on the Street

blocks.body: You found kittens without their mother. Don't rush to take them right away. In most cases, the mother cat leaves her babies for a few hours to find food and then returns.

blocks.heading: 1. Assess the situation
blocks.body:
Before intervening, answer a few questions.
Do the kittens look well cared for? • clean coat; • sleeping calmly; • lying together; • not crying constantly; • warm to the touch.
The mother is most likely nearby and will return soon.

Are there signs of danger? • the kittens are cold; • they are meowing loudly without stopping; • they are crawling off in different directions; • they are covered in flies; • they are lying near a road; • they are out in the rain; • there are injuries; • there is no safe shelter around.
In this kind of situation, help may be needed immediately.

blocks.heading: 2. Observe
blocks.body:
If the location is safe: watch the kittens for 3-6 hours from a distance.
Important: • don't stand right next to them; • don't touch the kittens; • don't scare the mother away.
The mother cat may not approach while she sees a person.

blocks.heading: 3. When you can't wait
4. If you had to take the kittens
blocks.body:
Pick the kittens up with gloves or through a cloth. If a kitten bites or scratches you so that it bleeds, wash the wound with soap and water and see a doctor.
First rule: warming up matters more than feeding. A chilled kitten cannot properly digest food.
Use: • a warm blanket; • a heating pad wrapped in a towel; • a bottle of warm water.
The heat source must not be hot. Kittens cannot crawl away or tell you they're too hot, so overheating is just as dangerous as hypothermia.

How to use it correctly: always wrap the heating pad in a towel or blanket; the heating pad should cover about half of the box so the kittens can move away from it if they get too warm; never place kittens directly on the heating pad; regularly check the temperature with your hand — it should feel pleasantly warm, not hot.

blocks.heading: 5. Don't feed them cow's milk
blocks.body:
It is poorly digested by kittens and can cause severe diarrhea. Use only kitten milk replacer.
If you don't have any on hand right now, first warm the kittens up and contact a veterinary clinic or shelter as soon as possible.

blocks.heading: 6. Estimate the approximate age
blocks.body:
Under 1 week: eyes closed; ears folded down; barely able to crawl. They need to be fed every 2-3 hours, including through the night (this is critically important!).
1-2 weeks: eyes starting to open; crawling more actively. Feeding every 3 hours.
3-4 weeks: starting to walk; baby teeth appearing. You can gradually start introducing wet kitten food.
Over a month old: walking confidently; playing; eating on their own. Still need a veterinary checkup.

blocks.heading: 7. After every feeding
blocks.body:
In kittens younger than 3-4 weeks, the bowel and bladder are not yet able to work fully on their own.
After every feeding, you need to gently stimulate the area under the tail with a warm, damp cotton pad or soft cloth, mimicking the mother's licking. This helps the kitten urinate and have a bowel movement. So prepare a puppy pad or cloth in advance.

blocks.heading: 8. How to house the kittens
blocks.body:
Prepare: a box; a soft towel; a warm shelter; freedom from drafts; quiet.
The ideal temperature depends on age: 0-1 week: about 30-32°C; 2-3 weeks: about 27-29°C; 4 weeks and older: about 24-26°C.
Make sure the kittens can move away from the heat source if they get too warm.

blocks.heading: 9. Be sure to have a vet examine them
blocks.body:
Even if the kittens look healthy. This should include: determining age; assessing weight; checking for dehydration; examining the eyes; checking for parasites; drawing up a feeding plan; determining deworming timing; setting up a vaccination schedule.

Go to the clinic urgently, don't delay a visit, if: the kittens are cold and won't warm up; they won't nurse; they cry constantly; they aren't moving; they are breathing heavily; there is blood; there is pronounced diarrhea; there is severe abdominal bloating; there is pus from the eyes or nose; there are seizures.

blocks.heading: Important
blocks.body: If the kittens are in a safe place, look well fed and warm, and are sleeping peacefully, it's best to observe from a distance first. In many cases, the mother cat returns within a few hours. Kittens should be taken only when their lives are genuinely in danger or you are certain the mother will not return. This improves the babies' chances of healthy development and reduces the risk of complications associated with hand-rearing.

If a cat repeatedly goes to the litter box, strains, cries out in pain, licks at the genital area, and produces very little urine or none at all, this is an emergency.

Urethral blockage is especially dangerous in male cats: it requires urgent veterinary care, because without treatment it can quickly become life-threatening.

An open mouth, rapid breathing, an extended neck, noticeably increased abdominal effort, noisy or wheezing breathing, and bluish or very pale gums are always a reason to go to the clinic immediately. Before you leave, keep the cat as calm as possible, don't force it to move, and don't try to "wait and see if it passes."

Drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, unsteadiness, labored breathing, lethargy, and seizures can all be signs of poisoning. Remove the animal from the source, keep the packaging, plant, or object involved, do not induce vomiting at home without a veterinarian's instruction, and contact a veterinarian or a poison control service immediately.

If a cat has swallowed thread, ribbon, a rubber band, a small toy, or another object, it may develop vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, refusal to eat, lethargy, pawing at its mouth, or straining in the litter box. If you can see a long object sticking out of the mouth or anus, do not pull on it: this can damage the intestines, and the animal needs to be examined urgently.

During a seizure, do not put your hands in the cat's mouth, do not try to hold it down, and clear away nearby hard objects so it doesn't injure itself. Time the seizure: if it is the first one, lasts several minutes, recurs, or the cat does not regain consciousness afterward, urgent help is needed; after the seizure, keep the animal in a quiet place and contact a clinic right away.

For heavy bleeding, apply sterile gauze or a clean cloth and maintain firm, direct pressure. If the dressing soaks through, do not remove it — add another layer on top and keep applying pressure; if a leg is bleeding, you can raise it above heart level on the way to the clinic.

Even if a cat gets up after a fall and seems "fine," it may have hidden injuries that show up later.
Until it can be examined, keep it warm, quiet, and moving as little as possible, especially if there is limping, pain, difficulty breathing, lethargy, or refusal to eat; after falls from a height, watch closely for signs of shock and head or chest injuries.

title: Injured by a Child: First Aid and Prevention

blocks.body: If a child has thrown, dropped or squeezed the cat hard and afterwards there is blood from its mouth, marked lethargy or apathy, or it seeks out warmth, this is a critical condition. Such signs very likely point to serious internal injuries: a head injury, damage to internal organs (lungs, liver), internal bleeding, or a broken jaw or ribs.

blocks.heading: Dangerous mistakes
blocks.body:
• Bathing a cat in shock. Washing is an extreme stress. In traumatic shock the body temperature drops fast, and a bath makes the chilling and the shock worse and can stop breathing or the heart.
• Treating the cat yourself on advice from the internet. Time spent searching for information when there are signs of internal bleeding or shock directly threatens the pet's life. Human medicines given without a vet's prescription are usually toxic to animals: paracetamol and metamizole (analgin), for example, are deadly for cats.

blocks.heading: Part 1. First aid
blocks.body: If you suspect a serious injury, the main task is to do no harm and to get the cat to a clinic as fast as possible.

blocks.heading: Step 1. Keep the cat calm
blocks.body:
• Settle the cat in a quiet, dimly lit, well-ventilated room.
• Put it in a carrier or a sturdy cardboard box with a flat, firm bottom lined with soft fabric.
• Do not shake, scold or keep moving the cat, and do not pick it up unless you have to.

blocks.heading: Step 2. Keep it warm
blocks.body:
• In traumatic and hypovolemic shock the body loses heat quickly.
• Gently cover the cat with a light blanket or towel.
• If the paws and ears are cold (a sign of hypothermia), put a bottle of warm water next to it, always wrapped in thick fabric so it cannot burn. Do not overheat the cat or use water that is too hot.

blocks.heading: Step 3. Check and hygiene
blocks.body:
• Do not wash the cat! No water procedures at all.
• If there is visible external bleeding, gently press a sterile wipe or a clean bandage to the wound.
• Put a bowl of fresh water next to the cat. Never force water or liquid food into its mouth: if the swallowing reflex is impaired or the head is injured, the cat can choke.

blocks.heading: Step 4. Get to a vet urgently
blocks.body:
• The cat needs to be examined by a vet in person without delay. Take it to the nearest veterinary clinic and carry it as gently as you can.
• If you physically cannot leave right away, contact a vet at once through an online consultation service: they will tell you how to stabilize the cat.
• Do not give any medicines from your home first-aid kit until a vet prescribes them.

blocks.heading: Part 2. Talking to the child and prevention
blocks.body: Children and pets living together need constant supervision and consistent upbringing.

blocks.heading: Step 1. Explain the consequences
blocks.body:
• Do not punish the child physically or shout: that only causes fear and aggression and teaches no understanding.
• Have a serious talk as equals. Explain that the cat is a living being and feels pain just like a person does.
• Use comparisons the child understands: "Remember when you fell and it hurt? The cat hurts even more now, but it can't tell us in words."

blocks.heading: Step 2. Set clear rules
blocks.body:
Agree on the limits and make sure they are kept:
• Touching. Not allowed: squeezing, throwing, pulling the tail, ears or paws. Allowed: stroking the back smoothly and lightly.
• Rest and sleep. Not allowed: waking the cat, pulling it out of its house or hiding place. Allowed: leaving the cat alone until it wakes up.
• Food and litter box. Not allowed: distracting, scaring, getting in the way. Allowed: simply staying away from the bowls and the litter box.
• Adult supervision. Not allowed: leaving children under 7 alone with the cat. Allowed: any contact only with an adult present.

blocks.heading: Step 3. Teach gentle contact
blocks.body:
• Show the child how to stroke the cat: with the fur, on the head and back.
• Explain which places must not be touched: belly, paws, tail, eyes and ears.
• Teach them to hold the cat properly: one hand supports the chest, the other supports the hind legs from below, so the cat never dangles in the air.

blocks.heading: Step 4. Build empathy
blocks.body:
• Involve the child in daily care for the cat, as suits their age.
• Give simple tasks: putting out dry food on schedule, changing the water in the bowl, tidying up the toys.
• Praise them for caring and being gentle.

blocks.heading: The main thing
blocks.body: Full responsibility for the pet's health and for safe contact between child and animal lies with the adults. Children cannot always judge their strength or understand the consequences of what they do. The parents' job is to create a safe environment, react in time when the pet's health is in danger, and teach children to treat living beings with care and responsibility.

If vomiting or diarrhea recurs, lasts more than a few hours, the cat becomes lethargic, cannot keep water down, or blood appears in the vomit or stool, urgent veterinary evaluation is needed.
This can be related to poisoning, infection, or an obstruction, and trying to "wait it out at home" increases the risk of dehydration and deterioration. Do not force the cat to eat or drink.

If an adult cat has not eaten normally for about 24 hours, and even much less time for a kitten, this is already a reason for an urgent visit.
• Cats that stop eating quickly develop an increased risk of fatty liver disease (hepatic lipidosis).
• Dry or pale gums, weakness, sunken eyes, infrequent urination, or refusal to drink make the situation even more urgent.

If a cat feels cold to the touch, is weak, drowsy, breathing poorly, unsteady, or stops responding, this may be hypothermia.
A cat's normal body temperature is approximately 38.0-39.2°C.
In case of hypothermia, move the cat out of the cold, dry it off, cover it, and warm it gradually using warm — not hot — heat sources, without rubbing the skin.

Sudden weakness, fainting, going limp, unresponsiveness, or collapse are always an emergency.
Check whether the animal is breathing and has a heartbeat; if it is not breathing, call an emergency vet clinic right away — the vet will tell you over the phone what to do while you are on your way.

Sudden weakness or paralysis of the hind legs, severe pain, cold or pale hind paws, and labored breathing can indicate aortic thromboembolism — this is an emergency condition. It tends to happen suddenly, is often accompanied by crying out in pain, and requires immediate help rather than waiting until morning.

Rapid open-mouthed breathing, bright red or very pale gums, vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, an unsteady gait, seizures, collapse, and loss of consciousness are typical signs of heatstroke. Move the cat to a cool place right away, cool it with room-temperature or cool water, do not use ice water or ice, do not force it to drink, and get to a veterinarian as quickly as possible.

Sudden swelling of the face or muzzle, hives, vomiting, diarrhea, restlessness, difficulty breathing, or sudden collapse can be signs of anaphylaxis.
This can develop very quickly after an insect bite, a vaccine, a medication, or another allergen, so you cannot wait: remove the possible source if it is safe to do so, and get the cat to a veterinarian urgently.

For a fresh burn or scald, cool the area with cool water or a damp compress as quickly as possible, but do not use ice and do not apply creams or ointments.
After cooling, keep the cat warm and calm and have it examined by a veterinarian as soon as possible; for a chemical burn, it's important to bring the substance's packaging along if possible, so the vet can understand its composition.
